title: Free Fall and Acceleration Due to Gravity

content.text: Free Fall and Acceleration Due to Gravity

Drop a stone from a tall building and watch it fall. It starts slowly and picks up speed as it descends — it accelerates. This acceleration is caused by gravity, one of the four fundamental forces of nature. Near the surface of the Earth, all objects experience a gravitational pull that causes them to accelerate downward at approximately the same rate, regardless of their mass.
This lesson explores the concept of free fall, the acceleration due to gravity (

), and what happens when air resistance comes into play. We will also introduce the basics of projectile motion and the concept of terminal velocity. Understanding gravity is fundamental to physics and will be built upon throughout your studies.
is the motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone, with no other forces acting on it. In true free fall, the only force on the object is its weight (the gravitational force).

In practice, perfect free fall only occurs in a vacuum, where there is no air resistance. However, for many everyday situations — especially when objects are dense and compact (like a stone or a ball) — air resistance is small enough that we can treat the motion as approximately free fall.
A key feature of free fall is that
all objects fall with the same acceleration

, regardless of their mass. This was famously demonstrated by Galileo (according to tradition, from the Leaning Tower of Pisa) and confirmed dramatically by the Apollo 15 astronauts, who dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon (where there is no air) and showed they hit the ground at the same time.

A skydiver falling in a spread-eagle position has a terminal velocity of about 55 m/s (about 200 km/h). When they pull their parachute open, the cross-sectional area increases enormously, air resistance suddenly exceeds weight, they decelerate, and a new, much lower terminal velocity (about 5 m/s) is reached.

The velocity-time graph for a falling object reaching terminal velocity shows a curve that starts steep (near the acceleration due to gravity) and gradually flattens out to a horizontal line at the terminal velocity.

Explain why a skydiver initially accelerates but eventually reaches a constant speed.

When the skydiver first jumps, their velocity is zero so air resistance is negligible. The only significant force is their weight acting downward, giving a net downward force and acceleration close to
As the skydiver speeds up, air resistance increases because it depends on speed. The net downward force (weight minus air resistance) decreases, so the acceleration decreases.
Eventually, air resistance equals the skydiver's weight. The net force is zero, so by Newton's first law, the skydiver moves at constant velocity. This constant velocity is the terminal velocity.
"Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects."

In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate. A 10 kg ball and a 1 kg ball dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time. The confusion arises because in air, objects with large surface areas relative to their weight (like feathers) experience significant air resistance and fall more slowly.
"Objects in free fall have no gravity acting on them."

Free fall means gravity is the only force acting. Astronauts in orbit appear weightless because they are in free fall — they and their spacecraft are both accelerating toward Earth at the same rate — but gravity is very much acting on them.
"At the top of its flight, a thrown ball has zero acceleration."
At the top, the velocity is momentarily zero, but the acceleration is still
(approximately 10 m/s² downward). Gravity does not stop acting just because the object has momentarily stopped moving.
"Terminal velocity means the object has stopped."
Terminal velocity is a constant speed, not zero speed. The word 'terminal' means 'final' — it is the final, constant speed that the object reaches.

In air, the feather has a much larger surface-area-to-weight ratio, so air resistance has a much greater effect, slowing it significantly. The coin is dense and compact, so air resistance is negligible. In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so both fall at the same rate under gravity alone.

The graph shows: (i) a curve from zero increasing steeply then levelling off to a horizontal line (first terminal velocity), (ii) when the parachute opens the velocity drops sharply, (iii) a new lower horizontal line (second, lower terminal velocity).

Both accelerate initially. Ball A (steel) has a high density and small surface area relative to its weight, so air resistance is negligible — it falls with acceleration close to $g$ throughout. Ball B (table tennis) is light with a relatively large surface area, so air resistance becomes significant quickly. Ball B reaches a lower terminal velocity sooner and hits the ground later and at a lower speed.
